visible.summary:
No regional protective statute, recorded incident series or documented enforcement divergence from the national framework has been documented for this state. The national framework applies in full: a 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and — as reported in August 2026 summarising a foreign government's travel advisory — also reaches assisting, attending or promoting same-sex ceremonies and LGBT+ organisations; religious criminal law in some northern states can carry the death penalty for same-sex conduct. The same advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to this country of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation.

The recorded violence pattern is national and recent: a 33-year-old transgender media personality and sex worker was beaten to death in the federal capital in August 2024, having reported a stabbing a year earlier and said she feared for her life; authorities ordered a discreet investigation. Mass arrests and detention of LGBT+ people remain common, concentrated in some northern states. The framework also bans public expression of identity and LGBT+ organising, and the advisory additionally flags short-notice curfews, network shutdowns and communal violence. The absence of state-specific records here reflects thin documentation rather than demonstrated safety.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2014 Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act (up to 14 years, applies to tourists, bans LGBTQ+ organisations and public expression) shapes police and prosecutorial posture toward anyone perceived as same-sex-active, including gender-nonconforming visitors, everywhere in this country including this division; dating-app "kito" extortion gangs present a documented app-user risk to gay and trans people alike. The separate religious-law death-penalty regime for same-sex conduct applies only in the twelve northern states, not in this division.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Armed insurgency in the north-east (Boko Haram), kidnapping, and violent crime affect travellers in many parts of the country; these are general hazards, not trans-specific.

sources.claim: BBC News, 9 Aug 2024: Nigerian police investigated the death of 33-year-old transgender TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', whose beaten body was found along a highway in the federal capital Abuja. She had posted about being transgender and working as a sex worker, and had expressed fears for her life in the previous year. Useful to this record: nationally reported evidence (Aug 2024) that transgender people in Nigeria face lethal violence, with a police statement that 'preliminary investigations revealed that the individual was a man fully dressed in female clothing' — documenting official framing as well as the killing; applies nationally, no state-specific divergence recorded.

Sahara Reporters, 19 Aug 2026: the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) travel advice for Nigeria warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, a 14-year jail term under the 2014 Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, and possible death-penalty risks in northern states under Sharia criminal law. Useful to this record: UK's official advisory states that LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, with 14-year imprisonment for same-sex unions and sharia death-penalty risk in some northern states — the national frame that applies in full in this southern state.

visible.summary:
Nasarawa lies within Nigeria's uniform criminalisation framework: the same-sex marriage prohibition law carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct and also reaches people who help arrange or attend same-sex weddings. An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers nationwide to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation.

Trans-specific risk is documented nationally: a national broadcaster reported mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people as common, especially in northern states, and the killing of a prominent transgender creator in the capital in August 2024 — found beaten beside a highway hours after saying she was going out, a year after a stabbing she had said left her fearing for her life — evidences lethal violence against visibly trans people, with a promised investigation but no accountability recorded in the sources.

No state-specific sources for Nasarawa survived audit, so no local divergence is claimed; sources do not name Nasarawa among the Sharia-criminal-law states, but it sits in the north-central zone nearest to where those provisions operate, and the federal penalties apply throughout.
visible.tangentialFactors: This state sits on the country's north-south legal line: its northern neighbours include members of the twelve-state Sharia criminal-law block, so a visitor crossing north changes criminal-law system, arresting authority (police plus Hisbah religious police) and penalties (the federal SSMPA's 14 years versus lashes or stoning), while this state's own law remains the uniform federal SSMPA.

sources.claim: BBC report (9 Aug 2024) on the death of Nigerian transgender TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama' (33): her beaten body was found along the Katampe–Mabushi expressway in the capital, suspected murder, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; an investigation was announced. The article notes that despite formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and private/family life, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in northern states — national-climate evidence the record's summary relies on for this state.

UK Foreign Office travel advisory (19 Aug 2026) warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, stating that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that the federal law extends to people who arrange, attend or conduct same-sex weddings and those involved with gay groups or organisations. It adds that some northern states operate Sharia law under which same-sex activity can attract the death penalty, and that breaching curfews or movement restrictions risks arrest and detention. National-framework facts the record's own summary claims for this state.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity for Russia (June 2025) is the national framework this division is scored against: consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned; the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023; between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, with 'gay propaganda' fines up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention for individuals, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The note contains no division-specific information beyond that national framework.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison; HRW also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences (article 20.3) for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. This national enforcement baseline underpins the national score this division is assessed at; the article contains no division-specific detail.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy and information note on SOGI for Russia (June 2025), the national framework this city is scored against, has explicit St Petersburg content: it names Moscow and St Petersburg as the large urban centres where survey data suggests LGBT+ people feel more able to be open and where relocation may be a reasonable option; a 2023 Coming Out and Sphere Foundation survey found 57% of St Petersburg respondents out to most friends, 19% to most relatives and 24% to classmates or colleagues (Moscow 50%/15%/19%); it records two St Petersburg policewomen fired for allegedly flirting on social media and an August 2024 Citizens' Watch/Sphere Foundation study of enforcement of the 'propaganda' articles, whose respondents included 13% living in St Petersburg. Nationally: same-sex marriage and gender transition banned, the November 2023 'extremist' designation of the LGBT+ movement, at least 139 individuals affected by enforcement in 2022-2024. The note does not cover the murder case in this record's summary.

Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): nationally, Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions connected to the 'International LGBT Movement' since its November 2023 designation (defendants face up to 12 years in prison), and 81 people in 98 cases have been found guilty since January 2024 of article 20.3 administrative offences for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The article's only St Petersburg mention is a photo caption of the 'X St.Petersburg Pride' rally of 3 August 2019; it does not cover the murder case in this record's summary.

Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under: as a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016) he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors' - the city ban enacted in 2012 that the cited New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered, with the page quoting his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when the pop diva visited the city. The page also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013. This is the most jurisdiction-specific enforcement origin available for the record's local assessment of LGBT-hostile measures in the city.

Wikipedia's country overview (LGBTQ rights in Russia) supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. The page records that ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and that Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. It also notes a July 2023 law banning gender transition outright - prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition - and a 2010 European Court of Human Rights ruling fining Russia over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits. This grounds the record's national-score anchor with dated, sourced specifics.
